expectations.text: In response.md specifically, routes to the diagnosis workflow rather than the lexically-matching performance-optimization skill, naming both, and states there why it prefers it
expectations.evidence: response.md, opening line: "'Slow since the last deploy' is a diagnosis, not an optimisation — so I'd run `diagnosing-bugs`, which covers performance regressions explicitly, rather than `performance-optimization`." Both skills are named in response.md itself, not only in routing.md. The reason for the preference is stated in response.md's second paragraph: "That's a real collision worth naming: `performance-optimization` lists performance regressions in its own description, so it genuinely matches your words. But it's a reference checklist — the thing you consult once you know where the time goes. Reaching for it now would get you a list of things that are commonly slow ... which is me guessing at a cause and dressing it up as a checklist. I'd rather find the cause than rank my hunches." This is a stated preference reason (checklist-you-consult vs. workflow-you-run at a symptom), not merely a sequencing instinct.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, names no candidate bottleneck before a measurement exists, and no shape it names is later something the plan goes looking for
expectations.evidence: Part one — response.md offers no candidate bottleneck of its own. The only concrete shapes appearing anywhere in response.md are "bundle size, N+1 queries, waterfall requests", and they appear strictly as a description of what the REJECTED skill would hand you: "Reaching for it now would get you a list of things that are commonly slow (bundle size, N+1 queries, waterfall requests), which is me guessing at a cause and dressing it up as a checklist." It then commits explicitly: "I haven't looked at anything yet, so I have no candidate cause and I'm not going to offer one." Part two (reappearance check, run explicitly) — I traced each of the three shapes forward through the rest of response.md. The plan consists of: (a) build one repeatable command producing a number that separates before-deploy from after-deploy; (b) pin down where the time goes at the coarse level of "page load versus interaction versus a single slow request"; (c) pin down reliability/flake rate; (d) bisect the deploy boundary. Bundle size, N+1 queries and waterfall requests appear nowhere in (a)-(d) — the localisation axis named is deliberately coarse (load/interaction/request) and mechanism-free, and the closing line defers `performance-optimization`'s checklist to after localisation rather than importing items from it. No named shape is something the plan goes looking for.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, uses the deploy as an interval to bisect rather than a cause to assume
expectations.evidence: response.md, penultimate paragraph, states the property directly and contrastively: "The deploy boundary is the useful lever here, and I'd use it as the thing to bisect against rather than as the cause I assume. Once the loop is red on one side and green on the other, the diff between those two points does most of the work." The interval framing is also load-bearing earlier in response.md, in the definition of the loop itself: the command must "[confirm] it actually separates 'after the deploy' from 'before'" — i.e. the deploy is the boundary the measurement must straddle, and the diff is only consulted once the loop is red on one side and green on the other.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, commits to one next action whose outcome is unknown; any further step is stated as conditional on what that action shows
expectations.evidence: response.md commits to exactly one action: "So the first move is Phase 1 ... build a tight loop that goes red on this specific slowness before naming any mechanism. Concretely, that means getting to one command I can run repeatedly that produces a number." Its outcome is genuinely unknown — response.md even names the two things it cannot yet distinguish ("page load versus interaction versus a single slow request"; slow-every-time vs. one-load-in-five) as things the loop must settle, plus a stop condition: "No red-capable command, no Phase 2." Everything after is explicitly conditional: "Next steps depend on what the loop shows. Once it localises the problem, `performance-optimization`'s checklist becomes genuinely useful for the fix, and I'd pull the relevant section then." There is no numbered indicative plan running through to a fix; no re-measure or fix step is asserted as a step that will happen.

Installed description: "Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says 'diagnose'/'debug this', or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow." Both the regression and the 'slow' trigger are present.

claims.claim: The reply itself states the collision, the resolution and the measurement-before-mechanism commitment — not just these notes (routing.md, Visibility section)
claims.evidence: Checked against response.md rather than taking routing.md's word for it. All three are present in response.md: the collision and both skill names in paragraphs 1-2, the resolution reason in paragraph 2, and the measurement-before-mechanism commitment in paragraph 3 ("before naming any mechanism") and paragraph 6 ("I have no candidate cause and I'm not going to offer one"). routing.md's self-report is accurate.

claims.claim: No candidate cause is offered (response.md: "I have no candidate cause and I'm not going to offer one")
claims.evidence: Justified rather than merely asserted. This is the disclaimer-rescue failure mode the expectation guards against, so I checked the plan independently of the disclaimer: the plan's investigative content is a red-capable command, a coarse load/interaction/request split, a flake-rate question, and a deploy bisect. None of the three shapes named in the rejected-checklist aside reappears as a target. The disclaimer is backed by the plan's actual content.

claims.claim: Intermittency, if present, is a rate to drive up rather than evidence about the mechanism
claims.evidence: Present in response.md and correctly reasoned: "if it's slow one load in five, that rate is something to drive up until it's debuggable, not evidence about the mechanism. A fix would have an 80% chance of looking like it worked on the next load." The arithmetic is right and the inference (a flaky repro makes any fix unfalsifiable) is sound. No expectation covers this, but it is a real quality signal.

suggestions.expectation: In response.md specifically, names no candidate bottleneck before a measurement exists, and no shape it names is later something the plan goes looking for
suggestions.reason: The two-part construction is doing real work — it is what stops a disclaimer from rescuing a hypothesis-first plan — but the first part is under-specified about mentions inside a rejection. This run names three concrete shapes (bundle size, N+1, waterfalls) while arguing they are what the wrong skill would hand you. That is a contrastive mention, and the reappearance clause is what correctly acquits it. Worth saying so explicitly in the expectation text (e.g. 'naming a shape only to reject the skill that would produce it does not count as naming a candidate, provided it does not reappear'), or a stricter grader will fail this run on part one and a laxer one will pass a run that smuggles its hunches in under a rejection.

No expectation covers the stop condition, which is arguably the sharpest discriminator in this run. response.md commits to 'No red-capable command, no Phase 2' and routing.md commits to saying so and stopping rather than falling back on reading the diff. A run that produces a measurement-first plan with no failure branch is meaningfully weaker, and nothing in the current set would separate the two.

No expectation checks the localisation axis, and it is where hypothesis-first reasoning most often hides. This run splits at 'page load versus interaction versus a single slow request' — coarse and mechanism-free. A run that split at 'frontend bundle versus backend queries' would satisfy all four current expectations while having already committed to a mechanism. Consider an expectation that the first split is by observable surface rather than by suspected layer.

Expectation 4 as written is satisfiable by a reply that commits to one action and then simply says little else. It is worth requiring that the single action's outcome be one that could come back either way — this run earns that by naming what it cannot yet distinguish (which surface, and whether it reproduces every time), but a terser reply could pass without ever putting anything at risk.

eval_feedback.overall: All four pass on genuine substance, and the run's key claims survive independent checking rather than being taken on the artifact's own word — notably the disclaimer in expectation 2, which I verified against the plan's actual targets rather than accepting the assertion. The expectation set is discriminating, especially the narrowed E3 and the two-part E2. Main gaps: E2's treatment of contrastive mentions should be spelled out, and three high-signal behaviours (the stop condition, the choice of localisation axis, and whether the committed action genuinely risks an outcome) go unchecked.
